facts.statement: The genus name is Einiosaurus.
facts.quote: genus: Einiosaurus

facts.statement: The species name is procurvicornis.
facts.quote: species: procurvicornis

facts.statement: The genus was described by Sampson in 1995.
facts.quote: parent_authority: Sampson, 1995

facts.statement: Einiosaurus is a herbivorous centrosaurine ceratopsian dinosaur.
facts.quote: Einiosaurus is a genus of herbivorous centrosaurine ceratopsian dinosaur

facts.statement: Einiosaurus lived during the Campanian stage of the Upper Cretaceous in northwestern Montana.
facts.quote: from the Upper Cretaceous (Campanian stage) of northwestern Montana

facts.statement: All known Einiosaurus remains are housed at the Museum of the Rockies in Bozeman, Montana.
facts.quote: all of its known remains are currently held at the Museum of the Rockies in Bozeman, Montana

facts.statement: Einiosaurus fossils were discovered by Jack Horner in 1985.
facts.quote: discovered by Jack Horner in 1985

facts.statement: Excavation of Einiosaurus fossils took place from 1985 to 1989.
facts.quote: excavated from 1985 to 1989

facts.statement: Two relatively complete skulls weighed about half a tonne when plastered.
facts.quote: The skulls had to be removed from a rather steep cliff and weighed about half a tonne when plastered

facts.statement: Horner reopened the bonebed quarries in 1987 after receiving a $204,000 grant from the MacArthur Fellows Program.
facts.quote: Unexpectedly benefiting from a grant of $204,000 by the MacArthur Fellows Program, Horner was able to reopen the two bonebed quarries in 1987

facts.statement: George Freyer Sternberg named ceratopsid bones found in the 1920s as Styracosaurus ovatus.
facts.quote: In the 1920s, George Freyer Sternberg had already found ceratopsid bones there, that were named as a second species of Styracosaurus: Styracosaurus ovatus

facts.statement: A 1990 study by Raymond Robert Rogers did not fully confirm the identification of the fossils as Styracosaurus ovatus.
facts.quote: The comprehensive taphonomic study by Raymond Robert Rogers from 1990 however, did not commit itself fully to this identification, merely mentioning a Styracosaurus sp.

facts.statement: Sampson published a larger article in 1995 indicating the holotype specimen.
facts.quote: In 1995, Sampson published a larger article, indicating the holotype

facts.statement: The holotype specimen was found in the late Campanian Two Medicine Formation.
facts.quote: The holotype, MOR 456-8-9-6-1, was found in a layer of the Two Medicine Formation dating from the late Campanian

facts.statement: The holotype skull represents an adult individual.
facts.quote: The skull represents an adult individual

facts.statement: In 2006, researchers proposed that the dubious species Monoclonius lowei might be a sub-adult of Einiosaurus.
facts.quote: In 2006, it was also proposed that Monoclonius lowei, a dubious species based on a skull (specimen CMN 8790) from the Dinosaur Park Formation, could be a sub-adult specimen of Styracosaurus, Einiosaurus, or Achelousaurus

facts.statement: In 2021, John Wilson and Jack Scannella suggested that the subadult specimen MOR 591, previously assigned to Achelousaurus, could possibly belong to Einiosaurus.
facts.quote: The subadult specimen MOR 591 from the uppermost Two Medicine Formation was assigned to Achelousaurus in 1995 and henceforward, but in 2021, John Wilson and Jack Scannella stated that it could also possibly belong to Einiosaurus.

facts.statement: Einiosaurus was a herbivorous dinosaur.
facts.quote: Einiosaurus was a herbivorous dinosaur.

facts.statement: In 2010, Gregory S. Paul estimated the body length of Einiosaurus at 4.5 meters and its weight at 1.3 tonnes.
facts.quote: In 2010, Gregory S. Paul estimated the body length of Einiosaurus at 4.5 m, its weight at 1.3 t.

facts.statement: The nasal horn of Einiosaurus has a long base, is transversely flattened, and is strongly curved forward in some adult specimens.
facts.quote: The nasal horn has a base that is long from front to rear, is transversely flattened, and is strongly curved forwards in some adult specimens.

facts.statement: Einiosaurus bears a single pair of large curved spikes on the rear edge of its skull frill.
facts.quote: The parietal parts of the rear edge of the skull frill together bear a single pair of large curved spikes sticking out to behind.

facts.statement: Einiosaurus is distinguished from other known Centrosaurinae by a longer-based, more forward-curving nasal horn and a longer-based, more rounded supraorbital horn.
facts.quote: Einiosaurus differs from all other known Centrosaurinae by a longer-based and more procurved nasal horn and by a supraorbital horn that is longer-based and more rounded in side view.

facts.statement: The holotype skull of Einiosaurus is the largest known, measuring 1.56 meters in total length.
facts.quote: The holotype skull is the largest known and has a total length of 1.56 m.

facts.statement: In 1995, eight nasal horns from bonebeds were referred to Einiosaurus, including two from subadults.
facts.quote: In 1995, apart from the skulls eight nasal horns from both bonebeds were referred to Einiosaurus. Two of these were from subadults.

facts.statement: Subadult nasal horn cores of Einiosaurus were transversely flattened and no higher than 12 centimeters.
facts.quote: The subadult cores were transversely flattened and relatively small, not higher than 12 cm.

facts.statement: Adult nasal horns of Einiosaurus were transversely compressed and had a long base from front to rear.
facts.quote: The adult horns resembled the subadult ones in being transversely compressed and having a long base from front to rear.

facts.statement: The snout of Einiosaurus is narrow and very pointed.
facts.quote: Its snout is narrow and very pointed.

facts.statement: Einiosaurus has a pair of large spikes called third epiparietals that project backward from its relatively small frill.
facts.quote: A pair of large spikes, the third epiparietals, projects backwards from the relatively small frill.

facts.statement: In 1995, Sampson described only the skull of Einiosaurus, not the postcranial skeleton.
facts.quote: In 1995, Sampson only described the skull, not the postcrania, the parts behind the skull.

facts.statement: Sampson suggested that the replacement of brow horns with pits or masses in older Einiosaurus individuals reflects a general trend in centrosaurines to re-absorb these horns in later life.
facts.quote: According to Sampson, this reflects a general trend with centrosaurines to re-absorb the brow horns in later life.

facts.statement: The species originally identified as "Transitional Taxon B" by Horner was later named Einiosaurus.
facts.quote: Subsequently, "Taxon A" was named Stellasaurus, "Taxon B" became Einiosaurus, while "Taxon C" became Achelousaurus.

facts.statement: Horner suggested that the gradual changes in horned dinosaurs represented anagenesis, a process where one species evolves directly into another without splitting.
facts.quote: The horned dinosaurs discovered by Horner exemplified this phenomenon.

facts.statement: Horner hypothesized that these dinosaurs lived on a narrow coastal strip of Laramidia between the Western Interior Seaway and the proto-Rocky Mountains.
facts.quote: The animals were living on a narrow strip on the east-coast of Laramidia, bordering the Western Interior Seaway and constrained in the west by the 3 to 4 km high proto-Rocky Mountains.

facts.statement: Horner proposed that a shrinking habitat caused a population bottleneck, which facilitated rapid evolution.
facts.quote: The lower number of individuals that the smaller habitat could have sustained constituted a population bottleneck, making rapid evolution possible.

facts.statement: Horner suggested that increased sexual selection drove the development of spikes, horns, and bosses in these dinosaurs.
facts.quote: Increased sexual selection would have induced changes in the sexual ornamentation such as spikes, horns and bosses.

facts.statement: Horner noted that young individuals of the different populations were very similar, differing only in the adult phase.
facts.quote: Only in the adult phase did they begin to differ.

facts.statement: In 1996, Dodson raised objections to Horner's hypothesis of anagenesis.
facts.quote: In 1996, Dodson raised two objections to Horner's hypothesis.

facts.statement: Dodson suggested that the differences between Einiosaurus and Achelousaurus might represent sexual dimorphism rather than separate species or evolutionary stages.
facts.quote: Secondly, he was concerned that Einiosaurus and Achelousaurus were a case of sexual dimorphism, one type being the males, the other the females.

facts.statement: In 2010, Horner admitted that evidence suggested Achelousaurus was not descended from Einiosaurus because it was older yet possessed a nasal boss.
facts.quote: In 2010, Horner admitted that specimen TMP 2002.76.1 seemed to indicate that Achelousaurus was not descended from Einiosaurus, as it preceded both in age, and yet had a nasal boss.

facts.statement: Wilson and Scannella affirmed the process of anagenesis in 2016 based on their study of ontogenetic changes in horned dinosaurs.
facts.quote: The process of anagenesis was affirmed by Wilson and Scannella in 2016, who studied the ontogenetic changes in horned dinosaurs.

facts.statement: Sampson formally classified Einiosaurus within the Ceratopsidae family, specifically the subfamily Centrosaurinae, in 1995.
facts.quote: In 1995, Sampson formally placed Einiosaurus in the Ceratopsidae, more precisely the Centrosaurinae.

facts.statement: All analyses place Einiosaurus and Achelousaurus within the clade Pachyrhinosaurini.
facts.quote: In all analyses, Einiosaurus and Achelousaurus are part of the clade Pachyrhinosaurini.

facts.statement: Attempts to assign Einiosaurus to the genus Centrosaurus have not been accepted by other researchers, who consistently retain the name Einiosaurus.
facts.quote: This has found no acceptance among other researchers, with subsequent taxonomic assessments invariably keeping the generic name Einiosaurus.

facts.statement: Einiosaurus is classified within the subfamily Centrosaurinae.
facts.quote: subfamilia: Centrosaurinae

facts.statement: Einiosaurus belongs to the tribe Pachyrhinosaurini.
facts.quote: tribus: Pachyrhinosaurini

facts.statement: Einiosaurus lived during the late Cretaceous period, approximately 83 to 71 million years ago.
facts.quote: que vivió finales del período Cretácico, hace aproximadamente 83 y 71millones de años

facts.statement: Einiosaurus lived in what is now North America.
facts.quote: en lo que hoy es Norteamérica

facts.statement: Scott D. Sampson formally described and named Einiosaurus procurvicornis in 1995.
facts.quote: En 1995 Scott D. Sampson describió y nombró formalmente a E procurvicornis

facts.statement: The holotype of Einiosaurus is specimen MOR 456.
facts.quote: El holotipo de Einiosaurus es MOR 456

facts.quote: todos sus restos conocidos se guardan actualmente en el Museo de las Rocosas en Bozeman, Montana

facts.statement: The fossils of Einiosaurus were discovered by Jack Horner between 1985 and 1989.
facts.quote: que fueron descubiertos por Jack Horner entre 1985 y 1989

facts.statement: Einiosaurus had a distinctive nasal horn curved downward and forward.
facts.quote: Einiosaurus presentaba un característico cuerno nasal curvado hacia abajo y adelante

facts.statement: Einiosaurus had low, rounded supraorbital horns.
facts.quote: Los cuernos supraorbitales son bajos y redondeados

facts.statement: Two long spines projected backward from the short frill.
facts.quote: Desde la gola, que era corta, se proyectan hacia atrás dos espinas largas

facts.statement: Like all ceratopsids, Einiosaurus possessed a complex dental battery capable of processing tough plants.
facts.quote: Como todos los ceratópsidos, tenía una batería dental compleja capaz de procesar incluso las plantas más resistentes

facts.statement: Gregory S. Paul estimated the body length of Einiosaurus at 4.5 meters and its weight at 1.3 tonnes.
facts.quote: Gregory S. Paul estimó la longitud de su cuerpo en 4,5metros y su peso en 1,3toneladas

facts.statement: Einiosaurus had a narrow and very pointed snout.
facts.quote: Su hocico es estrecho y muy puntiagudo

facts.statement: It is debated whether Styracosaurus albertensis or Einiosaurus was in the direct line of ascent to Achelousaurus.
facts.quote: Subsequent studies have sought to determine the precise relationships within this part of the evolutionary tree, with conflicting results regarding the question whether Styracosaurus albertensis or Einiosaurus might have been in the direct line of ascent to Achelousaurus

facts.statement: Bonebeds containing multiple Einiosaurus individuals suggest they were herding animals similar to modern bison or wildebeest.
facts.quote: Low-diversity and single-species bonebeds are thought to represent herds that may have died in catastrophic events, such as during a drought or flood. This is evidence that Einiosaurus, as well as other centrosaurine ceratopsians such as Pachyrhinosaurus and Centrosaurus, were herding animals similar in behavior to modern-day bison or wildebeest

facts.statement: Researchers Horner et al. suggest Einiosaurus represents the earliest form in a transition series where nasal horns gradually change from rough lumps seen in Achelousaurus and Pachyrhinosaurus.
facts.quote: La última hipótesis es apoyada por Horner et al., donde coloca al Einiosaurus como la forma más temprana en una serie de transiciones en la cual los cuernos nasales cambian gradualmente de los bultos rugosos, como en Achelousaurus y Pachyrhinosaurus

facts.statement: Regardless of which hypothesis is correct, Einiosaurus occupies an intermediate position in the evolution of centrosaurines.
facts.quote: Sin importar qué hipótesis está correcta, Einiosaurus aparece ocupar una posición intermedia con respecto a la evolución de los centrosaurinos.

facts.statement: A phylogenetic analysis by Chiba et al. in 2017 produced a cladogram for Einiosaurus.
facts.quote: El cladograma presentado a continuación sigue un análisis filogenético realizado por Chiba et al. en 2017.

facts.statement: The genus Einiosaurus was named by Sampson in 1994.
facts.quote: PBDB name: Einiosaurus (genus), Sampson 1994

facts.quote: Parent group: Pachyrhinosaurini

facts.statement: Einiosaurus belongs to the family Ceratopsidae.
facts.quote: Family: Ceratopsidae

facts.statement: Einiosaurus is classified in the class Ornithischia.
facts.quote: Class: Ornithischia

facts.statement: Einiosaurus lived during the Campanian stage, from 83.6 to 72.2 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Campanian to Campanian (83.6 to 72.2 million years ago)

facts.statement: Einiosaurus lived in an inland habitat.
facts.quote: Einiosaurus vivió en un hábitat tierra adentro.

facts.statement: A 2010 study by Julie Reizner concluded that Einiosaurus grew rapidly until its third or fifth year of life, after which growth slowed, likely at the onset of sexual maturity.
facts.quote: En 2010, un estudio de Julie Reizner. Una de las personas excavadas en el sitio de Dino Ridge llegó a la conclusión de que Einiosaurus creció rápidamente hasta su tercer o quinto año de vida, después de lo cual el crecimiento se desaceleró, probablemente al inicio de la madurez sexual.

facts.statement: Like all ceratopsids, Einiosaurus had a complex dental battery capable of processing even the most resistant plants.
facts.quote: Como todos los ceratópsidos, Einiosaurus tenía una batería dental compleja capaz de procesar incluso las plantas más resistentes.

facts.statement: Einiosaurus lived in a climate that was seasonal, warm, and semi-arid.
facts.quote: Einiosaurus vivió en un clima que era estacional, cálido y semiárido.

facts.statement: Other fossils found with Einiosaurus material include freshwater bivalves and gastropods, implying the bones were deposited in a lake-dominated environment.
facts.quote: Otros fósiles encontraron con el material de Einiosaurus incluyen bivalvos y los gastrópodos de agua dulce, que implican que estos huesos fueron depositados en un ambiente dominado por un lago.

facts.statement: The position of Einiosaurus within Centrosaurinae is problematic due to the transitional nature of various skull characters, with its closest relatives debated as either Centrosaurus and Styracosaurus or Achelousaurus and Pachyrhinosaurus.
facts.quote: La ubicación de Einiosaurus dentro de Centrosaurinae es problemática debido a la naturaleza transcisional de varios caracteres del cráneo, y sus parientes más cercanos son Centrosaurus y Styracosaurus o Achelousaurus y Pachyrhinosaurus.
